Definition: A vaccine is a medical treatment designed  to protect against certain diseases by stimulating the immune system to recognize and fight off pathogens (like bacteria or viruses). To mention a few:  1. Pharmaceutical Scientists: These professionals conduct research to discover, develop, and test new drugs. They work in laboratories, performing experiments to understand how compounds interact with diseases and the human body. This includes chemists, biologists, and pharmacologists.  2. Basic researchers: These people work in early stages of research, including chemists, pharmacologists and toxicologists.  3. Physicians: They contribute to early clinical trials, ensuring safety and measuring effectiveness.  4. Bioinformaticians: They utilize data analysis and computing to understand biological data, and help to find targets for new medicines.  5. Clinical Research Coordinators: They manage the day-to-day operations of clinical trials, ensuring adherence to protocols and data collection.  6. Principal Investigators (Doctors): These are the doctors who lead clinical trials, oversee patient safety, and make medical decisions related to the study.  7. Clinical Trial Participants: These are the volunteers who participate in clinical trials, providing essential data on the safety and efficacy of the new medicine.  8. Statisticians: They analyze the data that is collected during the clinical trials.  9. Regulatory personnel: People who ensure that the clinical trials are done in accordance to regulations.  10. Regulatory Affairs Professionals: These experts navigate the complex regulatory processes required to obtain approval from agencies like the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in the United States or the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in Europe.  11. Regulatory Agencies: Organizations like the FDA and EMA that review clinical trial data and determine if a drug is safe and effective enough to be approved for public use.  12. Quality control and Assurance professionals: These people make sure that the medicine can be produced in a consistent and safe manner.  13. Medical Science Liaisons (MSLs): These professionals serve as a bridge between pharmaceutical companies and healthcare providers, providing scientific information and education about new medicines.  14. Pharmaceutical Sales Representatives: They promote new medicines to doctors and other healthcare professionals, providing information on their benefits and usage.  15. Marketing and Communications Professionals: They develop and implement strategies to raise awareness of new medicines among healthcare providers and patients.  16. Pharmacists: Pharmacists play a key role in dispensing medicines, and also in providing information to patients and doctors.  17. Continuing Medical Education (CME) providers: These organizations provide education to doctors, to keep them up to date on new medicines.  and the list goes on and on.

Just as a chef is not required to know the molecular structure of ingredients, a doctor does not need to list vaccine components to be knowledgeable about their function. Therefore, a doctor's ability to name three vaccine ingredients is not a valid measure of their competence or expertise in medical science. You can also tell from their mannerisms that they have an anxious anticipation for certain talking points, or when they're arguing their "Gotcha" points. These individuals in particular, at least from what I have seen in previous episodes, are the most guilty of this. When people like this are invited onto the show there is no learning, no honest discussion, or critical thinking happening, they are simply there to debate for the sake of debating and they hold a unanimously incorrect opinion to goad people into arguing against them, then use talking points average people may not be knowledgeable on so they can feel some kind of superiority "Proving someone wrong". "The pivotal trials for the polio vaccine in 1954, a landmark achievement in public health, utilized a true double-blind randomized controlled trial design with a saline placebo, involving hundreds of thousands of children . This study provided definitive evidence of the vaccine's effectiveness in preventing polio. Similarly, early trials for the measles vaccine in 1968 included a saline placebo group to assess its efficacy and safety . The Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b) vaccine, which has dramatically reduced the incidence of serious infections in children, was also studied using a saline placebo as a control . Furthermore, trials for the mumps vaccine and the RA 27/3 strain rubella vaccine employed saline placebos to establish their safety and effectiveness . More recently, a 2020 trial evaluating a P2-VP8 subunit rotavirus vaccine used a saline placebo control to demonstrate its safety and efficacy compared to no intervention . Trials for new pertussis vaccine technologies have also utilized saline placebos to establish basic safety before comparing them to existing vaccines .     The concept of the "Saline Placebo Pyramid" aptly illustrates that many foundational vaccines underwent rigorous testing with saline placebos to establish their initial safety and efficacy . These well-established vaccines then often serve as active comparators in subsequent trials for newer or combination vaccines, as it would be unethical to administer a saline placebo and leave children at risk for preventable diseases when safe and effective vaccines already exist . Therefore, while not every single childhood vaccine trial has used a saline placebo, particularly in more recent decades where ethical considerations favor active comparators, the claim that no such testing has occurred is demonstrably false."

Companies exploit this bias with their branding, because they know consumers care more if a label can brags how "natural" it is than if it's actually proven more effectively healthy.  It's mainly based on positive associations with an aesthetic of nature,  which I myself find more appealing than imagining lab machinery.  Also it can feel more personally empowering, if a more "natural" remedy is more easily accessible or we're just relying on what our bodies already have.  But there's an abundance of plants and raw materials that are toxic.  And almost anything can be unhealthy in certain quantities.  So try looking beyond the simplistic categories of "natural" vs "artificial" and consider that every material has a chemical composition, and regardless of whether we ate it straight off the ground or put it through some process by hand or by machine to combine with different substances,  or precisely engineered it at a molecular level,  it's health benefits should still be verified as effective.  That's what the method of science should be used for.  Testing everything that matters to us, whatever the source.
